title: How Large Must a Model Be to Grok? A competition between memorisation and generalisation timescales
claim: Where the memorisation and generalisation timescale curves cross predicts the model size at which delayed generalisation first appears consistently.
layout: 3 side-by-side plots, left-to-right, dual y-axes with crossing dotted lines
description: Three line-and-scatter plots, labelled (a) p=97, (b) p=113 and (c) p=139. Each has parameter count on a log x-axis. The left y-axis is generalisation delay in epochs. The right y-axis is epochs on a log scale. A noisy orange curve shows epochs to generalise and falls slowly as models grow. A steeper purple curve shows epochs to memorise and drops sharply. Dots are coloured on a green-to-blue scale by model dimension, with a colourbar at the far right. The dots sit at zero for small models, then rise once models are large enough. Dotted red crosshairs mark where the orange and purple curves intersect. Each crossing is labelled with its parameter count (147,411; 192,742; 432,230) and its epoch value. The eye goes first to the crossing and the point where the dots lift off zero. The legend sits in the top-left of each panel.
caption: Generalisation delay and learning timescales across models of different sizes for three primes. Orange curve: epochs to generalise; purple curve: epochs to memorise a random dataset of the same complexity. The colour of each dot encodes its model dimension $d$, which is proportional to parameter count. Generalisation delay is taken as the minimum delay over ten seeds; timescale curves are arithmetic means of measured times. The dotted vertical line marks out $\widehat{P}_{cross}(p)$, the parameter size at which the timescale of memorisation intersects that of generalisation. Empirically, $\widehat{P}_{cross}(p)$ correlates with parameter count where generalisation delay first becomes consistently non-zero.
abstract: Despite a known dependence between grokking and model parameter count, how model capacity shapes grokking remains an open question. Focusing on small Transformers and modular arithmetic, we give a quantitative account of the relationship between model capacity and grokking as a competition between two timescales: generalisation ($T_{\text{gen}}$) and memorisation ($T_{\text{mem}}$). Building on prior formalisms for the empirical information capacity of Transformers, we define and measure $T_{\text{gen}}$ on modular arithmetic datasets and $T_{\text{mem}}$ on random-label datasets of equivalent complexity, and show that their intersection correlates with model sizes where consistent grokking begins. We also observe empirical laws for $T_{\text{gen}}$ and $T_{\text{mem}}$ as models and datasets scale, motivating their forms theoretically and finding that our model of $T_{\text{mem}}$ is consistent with prior observations that larger models tend to memorise faster. Moreover, extrapolating our empirical timescale laws predicted the existence of datasets for which no model of any size would consistently grok, a pattern supported on the modular arithmetic datasets of larger primes, demonstrating that our framework can make qualitative predictions out-of-distribution.
